I need to build a stub TreeBuilder subclass within the test class since TreeBuilder is package-private and abstract, so my test needs to live in the same package to extend it and override process(Token) to record tokens for assertions. I'm adding a note that tokens get mutated by reset() after processing, so I need to be careful that tests checking token type/name capture the needed data before that reset happens. I shouldn't guess about behavior not shown in the source, but Token itself is part of the codebase under test, so its public methods used in TreeBuilder—like reset(), name(), nameAttr()—are fair to rely on since they're directly referenced there. Without knowing the exact getter for the tag name, the safer path is to verify process() is called the right number of times and check the token type, confirming it's a StartTag or EndTag through instanceof checks on the nested Token classes rather than assuming getter method names. I should prioritize branch coverage over verifying exact token internals, so I'll focus tests on initialiseParse's null-input and null-baseUri exception paths, and on confirming valid parse setup populates doc, reader, tokeniser, stack, baseUri, and errors correctly. I'll also check the two-arg parse overload defaults to non-tracking errors, though I'm unsure how to verify that property directly. For the three-arg overload, I'll pass a tracking ParseErrorList and confirm the builder's errors field holds the same reference since it's package-accessible. For runParser, I'll use a RecordingTreeBuilder with a timeout-bound test to confirm the loop terminates properly at EOF without hanging, and I'll test processStartTag directly to confirm it returns the boolean from process(). I need to verify the token type enum names in jsoup's Token.TokenType—likely StartTag, EndTag, Comment, Character, Doctype, and EOF based on standard naming conventions, so I'll use those directly in my stubs. To reduce risk of relying on the enum name being exact, I'll switch to using instanceof checks against Token.StartTag and Token.EndTag classes instead, since those class names are guaranteed to exist in the source. I'll plan test cases for processStartTag with an Attributes object, processEndTag, and currentElement, noting that the stack remains null until initialiseParse is called. After initializing, currentElement() on an empty stack returns null, while pushing an element onto the stack makes it return that last element. I'm now worried about a subtle aliasing bug: since process() stores a reference to the same token object, and runParser calls token.reset() right after process() returns, any stored reference's state could get mutated post-storage — so by the time a test checks something like `last.type`, the object may no longer reflect what it was when process() actually ran, unless the tokeniser creates a fresh token instance each read. Looking closer at the loop structure, reset() is called right after process() but before the EOF break check happens, meaning the type field must survive reset() intact for that break logic to even work — otherwise the parser would loop forever on EOF. This is a direct logical deduction from the working implementation itself: reset() preserves type while clearing other fields like attributes or data, so checking `type == EOF` post-reset is actually safe and correct. My test adds each token to `seenTokens` inside process() before reset() runs on it, but since it's the same object reference, by the time the test assertions execute, every token has already been reset — so checking type on the last token is still valid since that field persists. I don't need to check type on earlier tokens since my other tests like runParser_multipleTokens only verify count anyway. For processStartTag_byName, since that method never triggers reset() at all, the instanceof check there is unaffected by any of this. I'm also confident the instanceof class check works regardless of reset state, since reset() doesn't alter an object's class. For the malformed input test with an incomplete tag, I'll trust the underlying Tokeniser/CharacterReader to handle EOF gracefully without throwing, especially since errors aren't being tracked by default. I'm fairly confident ParseErrorList.noTracking() and tracking(int) are both legitimate jsoup API methods.
